The Humboldt white-fronted capuchin, Cebus albifrons, is a Neotropical primate of considerable interest in comparative life-history studies. Field measurements indicate that females reach an ultimate body length of 37.5 centimeters [Li = 37.5 centimeters], a relatively modest stature for a cebid monkey. Neonates, upon parturition, have a recorded wet weight at birth of 233 grams [Wwb = 233 grams], placing them on the larger end of the altricial-primate spectrum typical of this genus. Under the stable thermal conditions of their equatorial forest habitat, where mean body temperature hovers near 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], the gestation period lasts approximately 158 days [tg = approximately 158 days]. This duration is comparable to that observed in other medium-bodied capuchins and appears tightly linked to the female's ability to sustain the demands of a rapidly developing foetus during the early dry season when fruit resources are most abundant.

Post-partum development in Cebus albifrons exhibits a clear sequence of maternal dependency. Suckling juveniles rely entirely on their mother's milk for the first several months of life, and the time since birth at weaning is recorded at 274 days [tx = 274 days] when individuals are maintained at a core body temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]. This prolonged nursing phase is thought to facilitate the complex social learning required for successful foraging on embedded invertebrates and hard-shelled fruits. Reproductive output is constrained by this extended period of maternal investment; females typically produce a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter], with a maximum observed frequency of approximately one litter every 1.4 years [F_R_i = approximately one litter every 1.4 years] under optimal conditions. This slow reproductive tempo, coupled with a relatively late onset of breeding, characterizes the species as a classic slow-life-history strategist among primates.

Sexual maturation in the white-fronted capuchin is a protracted process reflecting the need for extensive neurological and social development. Under the typical thermoneutral conditions of their tropical environment (38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]), the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 1310 days [tp = 1310 days]. This period of more than three and a half years before gonadal maturation is consistent with the pattern seen in other long-lived cebids, where young animals must master complex extractive foraging techniques and establish stable social hierarchies before they can compete effectively for mating opportunities. Adult males continue to gain mass and muscle long after reaching sexual maturity, ultimately attaining a maximum recorded adult body mass of 2400 grams [Wwi = 2400 grams], whereas adult females reach an ultimate wet weight of 2230 grams [Wwi = 2230 grams], a modest sexual size dimorphism that is typical of species where male–male competition is resolved through coalitionary alliances rather than direct combat.

Longevity data suggest that Humboldt's capuchin enjoys an extended period of reproductive viability in the wild. At a stable core temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C], the species is capable of a lifespan of 40.5 years [am = 40.5 years], which places it among the longest-lived of the platyrrhine primates. This remarkable longevity is thought to be supported by a combination of a high-quality, varied diet and complex social structures that buffer individuals against predation and disease. The extended period of senescence observed in this species, with females often continuing to reproduce well into their third decade, has important implications for understanding the evolution of post-reproductive life spans in New World monkeys, a topic that remains poorly resolved in the broader primate literature. Individuals in captive settings have occasionally surpassed this benchmark, though those records require careful interpretation.

From a comparative ecological perspective, the life-history of Cebus albifrons aligns closely with predictions derived from its relatively large brain size and extractive foraging niche. The modest sexual size dimorphism observed in this species, with males exceeding females by approximately 7% in body mass, reflects the coalitionary male strategy characteristic of capuchin social systems rather than direct male-male combat. Overall, the suite of life-history parameters observed in the Humboldt white-fronted capuchin including a prolonged gestation (158 days [tg = 158 days] at 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C]), a late age at first reproduction, and a high degree of maternal investment per offspring, underscores the selective pressures that have shaped the cognitive and social evolution of this lineage.
